title: Why Your Family Pays Everyone Back Except You

beats.text: You lend your brother three thousand dollars. Then you watch him pay every bill except yours.
His car payment clears. His phone bill clears. His credit card clears. You get nothing. Then your tire blows.
By the end, Dave has a repayment plan that protects his money without turning his brother into an enemy. The trick starts with one question.
Back in April, Danny's car died. Dave sent his entire emergency fund. Their contract was a pizza emoji. No date. No plan.
Danny still paid the car lender, phone company, and credit card. They could charge fees or damage his credit. Dave couldn't punish his brother. So Dave kept waiting.
Then Dave's tire blew, and he put four hundred dollars on his own credit card. That's when the family loan stopped feeling generous.
Quick guess: among people who lent money expecting repayment, how many lost money? Bankrate's twenty twenty-five survey said forty-four percent. Nearly one in two.
Danny might not be a villain. He might be broke too. But without a date and a plan, Dave is the easiest bill to postpone.
The IRS says evidence matters when deciding whether money was a loan or a gift. A written note and repayment schedule beat a pizza emoji.
So Dave calls Danny privately. They write down three thousand dollars, one hundred twenty-five a month, the day after payday, for twenty-four months. Both sign. Danny automates it.
Now Dave has a place in the payday line. Before lending again, he asks: is this a gift or a loan? If losing it would hurt, don't lend it casually. Give only what you can afford to lose as a gift.
One question. One page. No family courtroom at Thanksgiving. Subscribe for more money traps explained through Dave's disasters.
